title: Why Cities Are Getting Quieter
topic: Urban noise, and why measuring it is only half the problem
passage:
A
Ask people what they dislike about living in a city and noise will appear near the top of the list, usually above air quality and sometimes above rent. It is also the complaint that has been hardest to act on. Noise is invisible, it comes from everywhere at once, and until recently the main instrument available to a city was a limit that somebody had to be caught breaking. Yet the sound of urban Europe has begun, measurably, to fall — and the reasons have almost nothing to do with enforcement.

B
The largest single change is in the tyres, not the engine. At speeds below about thirty kilometres an hour a petrol car is dominated by the noise of its motor, which is why electric vehicles are so striking in slow traffic. Above that speed the sound a car makes is mostly the sound of rubber meeting road, and an electric car is no quieter than any other. Since most urban driving happens below that threshold, the shift to electric fleets has cut street noise substantially in exactly the places where people live, while changing almost nothing on the ring roads.

C
Road surfaces have done more than most residents realise. A porous asphalt, laid with deliberate air gaps, absorbs some of the sound generated at the contact patch instead of reflecting it, and can take several decibels off a busy street. The catch is maintenance: the gaps that absorb sound also collect grit, and a porous surface that has not been cleaned performs little better than a conventional one within a few years. Cities that laid it and then cut the cleaning budget found the benefit quietly disappearing.

D
The most contested measure has been the reduction of speed limits. Dropping a limit from fifty to thirty kilometres an hour reduces noise by roughly the same amount as removing half the traffic, because sound rises steeply with speed. Opposition tends to focus on journey times, which in practice lengthen very little in dense traffic where junctions rather than straights govern progress. What the measure cannot do is help where traffic is already slow, which is why it works better on through routes than in congested centres.

E
Buildings matter as much as vehicles. A double-glazed window fitted for warmth also cuts sound, but only if the two panes are of different thicknesses; identical panes resonate together and transmit certain frequencies almost unimpeded. Ventilation is the harder problem, since a room sealed against noise must be given fresh air some other way, and mechanical ventilation is expensive to install in existing housing. The result is a familiar trade in older flats: a quiet room or an open window, rarely both.

F
There is a limit to what any of this achieves, and it is not technical. Noise annoyance turns out to depend heavily on whether the person hearing it feels they have any say over it. Studies of residents near airports and railways have repeatedly found that two people exposed to identical measured levels report very different degrees of disturbance, and the difference tracks their sense of control and of fairness rather than the decibels. A neighbour's music at a level far below a passing lorry can be more distressing, because the lorry is nobody's decision and the music is somebody's.

G
This has an uncomfortable implication for planners, who are trained to work in numbers. A scheme that lowers measured noise by three decibels while being imposed on a neighbourhood may leave residents more annoyed than before, and a scheme that lowers it by one decibel after genuine consultation may leave them less. Some cities have begun to treat consultation as part of the acoustic design rather than a formality preceding it. Whether that counts as engineering or politics is a question the profession has not settled, but the evidence that it changes outcomes is now difficult to dismiss.

questions.instruction: The passage has seven paragraphs, A–G. Choose the correct heading for each of paragraphs B–F from the list of headings below. There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all.

sharedOptions.text: A surface that works only if it is looked after
Why the motor matters less than expected
How much noise costs a city each year
A measure whose effect depends where it is applied
Keeping sound out without sealing people in
Why identical exposure produces different complaints

questions.explanation: Paragraph B's point is that below thirty km/h the engine dominates but above it the tyres do, so electric cars help less than people assume. The engine — the motor — turns out to matter less than expected.

Porous asphalt absorbs sound, but “the gaps that absorb sound also collect grit”, so a surface that is not cleaned stops working. The heading has to carry the maintenance condition, not just the material.
Lower speed limits work on through routes and cannot help “where traffic is already slow”. The paragraph is about where the measure applies, which is what heading iv names.
The paragraph is about windows and the ventilation problem they create — “a quiet room or an open window, rarely both”. Heading v states exactly that tension.
Paragraph F reports that two people at “identical measured levels report very different degrees of disturbance”, and explains the difference by control and fairness.

questions.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.

questions.question: What is the main source of a car's noise at higher speeds?
questions.explanation: “Above that speed the sound a car makes is mostly the sound of rubber meeting road.” Rubber meeting road is the tyres, which paragraph B names in its first sentence. Either lift is accepted here: “rubber meeting road” or “tyres”.

questions.question: What collects in the air gaps of a porous road surface?
questions.explanation: “The gaps that absorb sound also collect grit.” The word is given directly and no synonym is needed.

questions.question: In dense traffic, what governs progress more than straight sections of road?
questions.explanation: The passage says journey times lengthen little “in dense traffic where junctions rather than straights govern progress”.

questions.question: For double glazing to block sound well, what must differ between the two panes?
questions.explanation: “Only if the two panes are of different thicknesses; identical panes resonate together.” The question asks what must differ, so the answer is the thickness.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.question: What does the writer say about electric vehicles?
options: They are quieter than petrol cars at all speeds
They help most on fast roads outside cities
They cut noise mainly in slow residential traffic
They have made road surfaces less important
questions.explanation: Electric cars are “striking in slow traffic” but “no quieter than any other” above about thirty km/h, so the benefit lands “in exactly the places where people live”.

questions.question: Reducing a speed limit from fifty to thirty is compared to
options: fitting new windows to every home
questions.explanation: The comparison is stated directly: the reduction “reduces noise by roughly the same amount as removing half the traffic”, because sound rises steeply with speed.

questions.question: Why is a neighbour's music sometimes more distressing than a lorry?
options: It is usually louder in measured terms
It is somebody's decision rather than nobody's
It occurs at frequencies windows cannot block
questions.explanation: The final sentence of paragraph F: “the lorry is nobody's decision and the music is somebody's.” Annoyance tracks control and fairness, not level.

questions.question: What is the writer's point in the final paragraph?
options: Planners should stop measuring noise levels altogether
Consultation may matter more to outcomes than small measured gains
Acoustic engineering has been shown to be largely ineffective here
Politics should be kept out of technical decisions entirely
questions.explanation: A three-decibel improvement imposed on people can annoy them more than a one-decibel one after real consultation — so consultation belongs inside the design, not before it.
